summary: Describes how to change the bandwidth and possibly other parameters of an already established CR-LSP using CR-LDP, without interrupting the traffic on it. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: If you need a bigger pipe for water already flowing, you do not want to shut it off. This shows how to widen a network path without stopping what flows through it.

questions: how to modify an lsp with cr-ldp
how does cr-ldp reroute an lsp
subtitle: How to change the bandwidth, route or priority of a live CR-LDP label switched path without tearing it down.

tldr.problem: After a CR-LSP is set up, an operator may need a different bandwidth, service class, route or priority, but releasing the LSP would interrupt the traffic it carries.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress sends a new Label Request carrying the same LSPID and the modified values, routers reserve only the bandwidth difference, the ingress switches to the new label, and then releases the old one.
tldr.outcome: The LSP is changed without service interruption and without double booking bandwidth. The RFC also gives an example of using it for dynamic bandwidth management.

facts.label: Concurrent modifications
facts.value: Not allowed before the previous one completes

today: RFC 3214 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It relies on the CR-LDP base specification in RFC 3212 for the modify flag.

sections.title: Why Modify a Live LSP
sections.content:
Take an LSP called L1 that was set up with traffic parameters T0, with bandwidth reserved along its path. Its bandwidth may need to grow to carry more traffic, or the SLA tied to it may change because a different service class is wanted. The operator wants to move L1 from T0 to T1 without releasing the LSP, which would interrupt service.

Operators may also want to reroute a CR-LSP to a different path for better performance or better use of network resources. The RFC uses the existing LSPID concept in CR-LDP to do all of this without interrupting service and without double booking bandwidth. An action indicator flag of modify states the behavior explicitly and leaves the LSPID free to support other capabilities later. That flag is specified in RFC 3212.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine changing the size of a road while cars are still driving on it. This memo explains how to do that for network paths so nobody has to stop.

sections.title: The Basic Modification Procedure
sections.content:
Modification is allowed only when the LSP is already set up and active. It is not defined during establishment or during label release or withdraw. Only the ingress LSR may request it, and it cannot start a new modification before the previous one has completed.

The ingress LSR R1 holds an entry in its FTN table mapping FEC1 to Label A. To modify L1, R1 sends a Label Request message with the new requested values and an LSPID TLV carrying the original LSPID. The Traffic Parameters TLV, the ER-TLV, the Resource Class (color) TLV and the Preemption TLV may differ from the original request. So bandwidth, service class, route and setup and holding priorities can all change.

Each LSR on the path treats the message like any Label Request, except that it checks whether it already has that LSPID. If it does, it computes the new bandwidth and reserves only the difference, which prevents double booking. It also assigns a new label. When the Label Mapping comes back, R1 has two outgoing labels, A and B, for the same FEC. It activates FEC1 to Label B and so moves traffic to the new label.

R1 then sends a Label Release carrying the LSPID and the Label TLV for the old label. Each LSR sees that the LSPID still has another label set, so it releases the old label without releasing the resource in use. If bandwidth went down, the delta is released. Then the modification is complete. The other LSRs need no new procedures to track old and new characteristics.
sections.plainLanguage: The first router builds a second, better path next to the old one, using the same name tag so everyone knows it is the same road. Once the new road works, traffic moves over and the old road is taken down.

sections.title: Rerouting an LSP
sections.content:
The same machinery can move an LSP to a different route. The ingress sends a Label Request with the same LSPID, an Explicit Route TLV with different hops, and the action indication flag set to modify.

Routers along the old and new routes behave as in the basic procedure. At the router Rj where the new route diverges from the old, the request is forwarded along the new route and is treated as setting up a new LSP by each LSR until the paths converge at a later router Rk. The modify value of the flag is ignored in between. Where the routes coincide, two label sets exist for the LSPID. Where they diverge, only one set exists.

When the Label Mapping reaches R1, it activates the new entry (FEC1 to Label B) and deactivates the old one (FEC1 to Label A). It then sends a Label Release along the original route. Between Rj and Rk only the old labels exist, so the LSPID TLV does not need to be examined to find the right label, but it must still be updated and passed on so that Rk knows which label to release and can keep forwarding the release along the old route.
sections.plainLanguage: Moving to a new route is like taking a detour. The two roads share some stretches and split apart in others, and when you finish, only the old detour-only parts are closed.

sections.title: Priority and Failure Handling
sections.content:
The setup priority in a modification Label Request may differ from the one used before. This effectively sets the priority of the modification request, and operators can pick it from their own policies. For example, if a customer has exceeded the reserved bandwidth of its VPN LSP tunnel by too much, the modification may be given a higher value. A modification can also carry a different holding priority. The LSR then assigns the new holding priority to both the existing labels and the new labels for the LSPID, which prevents self-bumping.

A modification can fail, for example because of insufficient resources. A Notification message is then sent back to the ingress, and the operator may retry. If the original LSP fails during a modification attempt, the attempt should be aborted with the Label Abort Request message from the LDP specification. After any modification failure, all modifications to the LSP, including the holding priority, must be restored to their original values.
sections.plainLanguage: If the bigger road cannot be built, the router sends back a note saying so, and the old road stays exactly as it was, so nothing is lost.

sections.title: Example: Dynamic Bandwidth Management
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example in which customers or services are assigned to CR-LSPs with one of three priorities: key, normal or best effort. The operator does not want to bump any LSP during setup, so holding priorities are all set to the highest value. Each link is given a current threshold priority Pi, meaning no bandwidth is available there for a Label Request with a setup priority lower than Pi.

To change the bandwidth of an LSP L2, the operator assigns a modification priority Mp by policy and the ingress sends a Label Request with Setup Priority = Mp. If bandwidth is sufficient and Mp is numerically smaller (higher priority) than Pi, the request is accepted. Otherwise it is rejected with a Notification indicating insufficient resources.

The RFC says this threshold scheme is implementation specific and only illustrates the flexibility of the procedure. It also describes giving a lower priority to bandwidth increases on a secondary-path LSP, and to an LSP that has exceeded its reservation.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a club with a bouncer. VIP requests get through even when the room is nearly full, but ordinary requests are turned away until there is space.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's security section is one sentence: protection against modification of LSPs by malign agents has to be controlled by the MPLS domain. The memo adds no authentication or protection of its own.

The Intellectual Property section also notes that the IETF has been notified of intellectual property rights claimed for some or all of the specification, and points readers to the online list of claimed rights.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not lock the door itself. It says the network's own owners must keep outsiders from changing the paths.
